summary:
Sol Keepers is a free browser game where kids ages 7–12 run a Mars outpost for 30 sols. Players place solar panels, batteries, an oxygen maker, a greenhouse, a storm shelter, a science lab and a comms dish, then decide how to share limited power between air, food, safety and science. No choice is free: sheltering from a solar storm drains power and stops research, and bonus science costs oxygen, power or food.

The hazards come from real NASA data. Solar storms replay actual events from the DONKI space weather database for May 2024, each shown with its date and event ID, and one storm uses the radiation dose Curiosity measured on Mars on May 20, 2024. An in-game panel lists every source, including studies from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository, and separates real measurements from simplified game rules.

It matters because most space content for kids shows mission outcomes, not the decisions behind them. Sol Keepers lets children feel the trade-offs mission planners face, in plain language, with no download or account.
details:
What it does and how it works

Sol Keepers is a browser game where players aged 7–12 command a Mars base with four crew for 30 sols (Mars days). They build on an isometric map using seven buildings: solar panels, batteries, an oxygen maker, a greenhouse, a storm shelter, a science lab and a comms dish. Everything runs on one shared power supply, so players keep deciding what matters most. Should the crew shelter from a solar storm and lose a day of research, or keep working and absorb the radiation? Should the base spend 30 oxygen on a spacewalk for bonus science? Time runs in real time and pauses automatically when an event arrives, so younger players have time to read and decide.

The hazards come from real NASA records. Each sol replays one real day of May 2024, the most intense solar storm period in two decades. Solar storms match actual DONKI particle events and show their dates and event IDs. A radio blackout follows the real X8.7 flare of May 14. One storm uses the 8,100 microrays that Curiosity measured on Mars on May 20, 2024.

Benefits

  • Players learn by deciding, not memorizing. Every choice has a cost, which mirrors how mission planners actually work.
  • Science terms such as sol, radiation dose and millisievert are explained in one sentence the first time they appear.
  • It runs in any modern browser on a computer, tablet or phone, with no download, account or cost.
  • Failure isn’t punishing. The crew evacuates safely, and the game explains what went wrong and suggests what to try next.
  • Classrooms can check the science. A built-in panel links every NASA source and lists which rules were simplified for gameplay.

Intended impact

Most space content for children shows what missions achieved, not the decisions behind them. We want kids to leave understanding one real constraint: in space, safety, survival and discovery all draw on the same limited resources. Because the storms are real dates, the game also shows that space weather is something NASA actually tracks.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in one self-contained file, with no frameworks or libraries.
  • The HTML Canvas 2D API for the isometric map, the hand-coded building designs and the visual effects. The game uses no image files.
  • NASA data from DONKI, NASA JPL mission releases, the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and NASA Goddard, stored inside the game as a labelled archive.
  • Node.js to simulate cautious, balanced and reckless strategies and check that the game is winnable, that no strategy is free, and that reckless play fails.
  • GitHub for hosting the code.

What makes it creative

  • The calendar is real: sol 9 of the mission is May 9, 2024 on the Sun, so kids play through a historic solar storm as it happened.
  • The 4–24 minute Earth–Mars signal delay becomes a game rule. Without a comms dish, storm warnings from Earth arrive almost too late.
  • The storm shelter turns radiation protection into a visible choice between safety and science.
  • A dust storm modelled on the one that ended the Opportunity rover’s mission cuts solar power to a quarter.
  • Every building is drawn in code, and each one shows its state: battery bars show real charge, and the greenhouse glows at night when it has power.

Factors we considered

  • Age group: three resources (power, oxygen, food) plus radiation, rather than a long list of systems, following the challenge guidance.
  • Accuracy: real data where we had it, and the game says clearly which numbers are real and which are game rules. The archived data is never presented as live.
  • Reliability during judging: the game doesn’t depend on a live connection, so it can’t break if an API is down or rate-limited.
  • Replayability: dust storms and bonus science events change every game, and different strategies lead to different results.
  • Accessibility: touch and mouse both work, there’s no keyboard requirement, the map scrolls on phones, and an optional tutorial teaches the controls in three steps.
  • Fairness: no choice is free, and no strategy wins without trade-offs.
